No, that's not right, and it matters for your design.

A language model remembers nothing between calls. Each time your program calls it, the model sees only the text you send in that call, which is its context. Then it writes a reply and forgets the call.

Chatbots seem to remember because the app re-sends the earlier messages every time. That's easy to mistake for memory in the model.

Here's an example. A student tells your assistant on Monday, "I finished the laser cutter safety training." On the next Monday, a new session starts with an empty context. If your program doesn't put that fact in front of the model, the assistant has no idea. It will ask again, or it will guess.

So memory between sessions is something you build:
1. Your program saves what matters, such as the student's training status, in a file or database.
2. At the start of the next session, your program loads it and puts it into the context.

The model can only use what is in its context. This also affects your budget, because everything you load costs tokens on every call.

This is the next topic in your mission, and it's the same decision you listed as a goal: what the assistant keeps in context, what it saves, and how it finds the right page in a long manual.

Quick question to check it landed: if the assistant should know a student's training status at the start of every visit, which part of the system does the remembering, the model or your program? What would it have to do?

I can write a lesson on context and memory for the makerspace assistant if you want one.
